title: Chapter 100 – The Rival Test
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

Inspector Dai walks the whole Garden twice, and finds nothing, and takes four hours to do it.

He walks slowly, with his thumbs hooked in his sash and a clerk at his heels writing down every word. He peers into the granary and the east kitchen, counts the beds, lifts the lid of the well, taps the wall of the forge with a jade-ringed knuckle. The six riders in silver and black sit their gray horses at the gate, motionless, with their hands resting on their thighs. They do not dismount. They do not speak. Once, when Pebble puts its snout out of Jian's collar to look at them, one rider's head turns a fraction, and a pair of flat eyes rests on the lump in the cloth, and moves on.

The Registry's escort, Jian thinks. Not Enforcement. Not Rong's people. He has seen the silver-and-black before only on the sleeves of a clerk.

In the forge, Hu is hammering a hinge.

He has been hammering the same hinge since dawn. It is a piece of ordinary iron on an ordinary anvil, and the sound it makes is the ringing, honest clang of any forge master's shop. The three quiet blades hang on the wall in a row, rubbed gray with ash, dull as old tools. Beside them is a rack of rusted pruning knives. The coupling plate is in Jian's sleeve, wrapped in cloth, pressed against his ribs. Feng stands in the corner, big and sullen, doing his best to look like a man who has never had an idea.

"A flue," says Dai.

"A chimney fire," Hu agrees, without turning. "It fell in. I cursed it for three hours and put it out with sand. You may look at the sand."

"I have looked at the sand." Dai stoops to a pail by the hearth, and sifts a pinch through his fingers. He smells it. He wipes his hand on a silk handkerchief, with care. "The array on the Mountain Gate recorded a null in the Garden's signature for four hours and eleven minutes. It is the first such null in the Garden's history. A flue does not make a null."

"A flue does if it fills the shed with smoke and the Qi in the smoke is poor," says Jian mildly. "I have read the Sutra Hall's treatise on coal-gas. It says wet ash can dampen a signature for as long as the fire burns."

Dai turns. His round face is perfectly pleasant.

"Gate Bearer. You are home on a pass."

"On the new moon, Inspector. As the Elders allow."

"A coincidence, then. That you should be here on the night of the first null in the Garden's history."

"I sleep poorly, and I came to help my family with the chimney. It is a clan custom."

"A dutiful son." Dai considers him for a long moment. Then he smiles. "I will record it so. A flue fire, a family custom, a null of four hours and eleven minutes, attributed to wet ash." He tucks the handkerchief into his sleeve. "I would suggest the Garden install a second chimney. It would be a pity to have the Court's array alarm again."

"We will see to it."

"Do." Dai turns to leave. At the door, without looking back, he adds in a pleasant undertone: "Gate Bearer. A word from the Registry, which is not the Court. They would be glad if you would attend the Midsummer Trial. All Silver Leaf disciples are required, but there is a particular wish that you be present."

"I had intended to."

"Good. They are very fond of intentions." He lifts a hand in farewell. "Go well."

The six riders wheel as one and follow the chair up the hill.

When they are out of sight, Hu lets the hammer fall. He stands there for a while with the iron ringing in the quiet, and then he says, very softly, to the anvil:

"They did not look at the walls."

"No," Jian says.

"They looked at you."

"Yes."

"Why?"

He has been asking himself the same question since the dawn. He does not have an answer. He has only the cold feeling that a hand was laid on the back of his neck and then lifted, gently, to show that it could be laid there again.

* * *

The challenge is posted on the morning of the Midsummer Trial's eve.

It hangs on the notice-board of the long hall, a single sheet of cream paper in a hand that is bold and fluent and quite beautiful. Jian reads it standing in the crowd of Silver Leaf disciples, with a bowl of millet cooling in his hand.

Under Article seventeen of the Inner Court Rule, I, Shen Yuhang of the Cloud Peak Hall, Silver Leaf, Foundation Middle, do challenge the provisional standing of Lin Jian, Gate Bearer, to a Trial of Position, to be held in the Ring of the Inner Court on the day of the Midsummer Trial, at the third bell. The terms are the Rule's. The stake is the standing.

A murmur runs through the hall.

He has read Article seventeen. Every disciple has. It is the oldest and least used clause in the Inner Court's Rule: A disciple whose standing is held by surety may be challenged by any disciple of equal or higher tier, and if the challenger prevails, the surety is forfeit.

The surety is Qin Hao's name.

He is not after me, Jian thinks, with a clean cold clarity. He is after the Guard. If I lose, the Rule requires Qin Hao's stake to be struck. His seat. His post. His name. And the floor will be tied no longer.

Someone touches his elbow. It is Tan Ruyan, in the silver-edged gray, with her jade pin and her level dark eyes. She says nothing for a moment. She looks at the notice.

"He has been planning this for months," she says quietly.

"I know."

"His family has wanted the Guard's seat for three generations. The Cloud Peak Hall is Core-bound. They hold two Elders on the floor and a Core Elder in seclusion. Qin Hao is the only voice in the Sect that is not theirs, and not Mu's, and not the Treasury's." She does not look at him. "He is a Foundation Middle swordsman at twenty-six, with the finest sword-form in the Inner Court. He has never lost a Ring match."

"I have never won one."

"I am aware." A faint, unamused twitch of her mouth. "I would advise you to decline."

"Article seventeen does not allow it."

"Then I would advise you to lose gracefully."

"If I lose, the surety is forfeit."

"I know." Her voice is very low. "I said it, and I do not like it."

He puts down the bowl. He is aware, in the oddly sharp way of a man about to be shot at, of the smell of millet and wood smoke, of the sunlight in the hall, of a bird singing on the ridge. He is aware of the sheet of cream paper and the fluent hand.

"Thank you," he says. "For telling me."

"I owe you a favor." She turns to go. "I had not meant it to be this one."

* * *

Bai hears him out in the dispensary, with a plum in one hand and a pestle in the other.

"Article seventeen," he says. "Hm."

"You know it."

"Everyone knows it. It has been used twice in my lifetime, and both times the challenger won." Bai grinds. "You are a Foundation Early. He is a Foundation Middle. You have no sword. You have never been in the Ring. I would normally say you are a dead man, and I would offer to prepare a very nice funeral tea."

"And abnormally?"

"Abnormally," says Bai, "I have been reading Article twenty-two." He sets down the pestle. His small shrewd eyes gleam. "The Leveling Brew."

"I do not know it."

"No one does. It is the Pill Hall's article. It has not been invoked in a hundred and sixty years, because no one remembers it exists. But it is there, in black and white, in the Rule." He takes a thick book down from the shelf and flips it open. "In any Trial of Position, the lesser party may request of the Pill Hall a brew, to be taken by both combatants before the bell, that the contest may be decided on equal footing. The brew shall reduce the Qi of each to the lowest rank among them, for the length of one stick of incense. Neither may refuse."

Jian reads it twice.

"Both combatants."

"Both. Shen would drink it too. He would fall to Foundation Early, my boy, the same as you. Not a hair more." Bai smiles. It is not a nice smile. "The brew is not hard to make. A few roots, a binding salt, a pinch of moss. I could brew a batch tonight."

"And Shen cannot refuse."

"If he refuses, he forfeits. If he accepts, he fights you on equal Qi." The old Elder spreads his hands. "Which is to say, as a man with a very fine sword-form and no great advantage in power, against a man who has endured Kuang's pole every morning for a year."

"That is a narrow edge."

"It is the only edge you have." Bai bites the plum. "Do not squander it."

* * *

Kuang finds him on the lawn at midnight, practicing alone.

He has not been able to sleep. He has come out in his shirt, with a practice staff and the dim light of the stars, and for an hour he has run the same three forms against an imaginary opponent, until his arms ache and the sweat has soaked through to his belt. The lawn is silent. The pool in front of the hall holds a few bright pieces of moon.

"Wrong," says a flat voice behind him.

He turns. The big woman stands under the pine at the edge of the grass, her arms folded, a shadow in the dark. She must have been there for some time.

"Tutor."

"You are guarding your head. You should be guarding your center." She comes forward, takes the staff from his hands, and weighs it in one fist. "A swordsman does not go for the head. He goes for the places that bleed. Thigh. Forearm. Side." Her flat eyes are on his face. "You will not win in the open. You are not fast, and he is. You cannot beat a blade with a pole."

"Then how?"

"You do not beat it." She hands the staff back. "You make him afraid of the one place he cannot cut."

"The shoulder."

"The left. The side of the heart." She taps his collarbone with one hard finger. "Your bones are clean. I told you. A year of my pole has made a thing that rings, and a blade that strikes it does not know what it has hit. It will want to withdraw. For a breath. That is all you need."

"I may not live to use it."

"You will. I do not hit my pupils for pleasure." She turns to go. Then, without looking back: "He will draw first. He always does. Take the first thrust on the left, and do not flinch. You will bleed. You will not break."

"And then?"

"And then," says Kuang, "hit him on the ankles. Everybody forgets the ankles."

She disappears into the dark. Jian stands on the lawn with the staff in his hands, and the stars turning overhead, and for the first time in two days his heart is steady.

* * *

The Ring of the Inner Court is a circle of white stone, thirty paces across, set in the center of a lawn.

It is surrounded on all sides by tiers of benches, and on the day of the Midsummer Trial every bench is full. Disciples in gray and silver. Elders in their dark robes, seated in a row under a canopy of blue silk. Servants, stewards, clerks. In the front tier, on a cushion of honor, sits Qin Hao, very upright, with his beard combed and his hands in his sleeves. He does not look at Jian. He looks at the sky.

The Arbiter strikes his staff on the stone. The crowd quiets.

"Under Article seventeen," says Shen Wuye, "a Trial of Position is called. The challenger, Shen Yuhang of the Cloud Peak Hall. The defendant, Lin Jian, Gate Bearer. The terms of the Rule apply. The weapon of the challenger is entered as a sword of the Cloud Peak Hall, registered at the Sect's armory. The defendant has no weapon."

"The defendant requests a staff," says Jian, in a clear voice.

"Granted. A practice staff, from the Ring's stores." The Arbiter nods to a steward, who brings one. It is plain ash, six feet, and heavy. Jian takes it. It is the same sort of pole that Kuang beats him with every dawn.

"The defendant," he continues, "also invokes Article twenty-two."

The crowd stirs.

Shen Yuhang, at the far side of the Ring, does not move. He is dressed in white and silver, with his hair bound and his sword at his hip, and the sun catches the hilt. His face is a pale carved mask. But a very small crease has appeared between his brows.

"The Leveling Brew," says the Arbiter slowly. "I had thought the article forgotten."

"The Pill Hall has not forgotten it," says Bai, rising from the Elders' row with a heavy wooden tray in his hands. On it are two small cups of gray ceramic, each filled with a thin green liquid. "I have prepared two doses. They are identical. The combatants may choose."

Shen's lip curls. But he is a man who has studied the Rule, and the Rule is clear. He walks to the tray. He looks at the cups. He looks at Jian.

"You have been busy, Gate Bearer."

"I had a good teacher."

"Of the Rule?"

"Of patience."

Shen lifts a cup. After a heartbeat Jian lifts the other. They drink together.

It tastes of bitter moss and salt. It goes down like a cold hand, and the effect is immediate: a draining, a settling, as if a tide had gone out of his body. The Qi in his dantian, the Foundation base, the six-sided stone, holds, but the river that feeds it runs thin. He feels it fall. He feels the whole world narrow. And across the Ring he sees Shen Yuhang's face change, just slightly, as the Foundation Middle Qi that has made him a prodigy since boyhood drains out of him, step by step, and leaves him standing in the sunlight a Foundation Early like any other.

"Begin," says the Arbiter.

* * *

Shen Yuhang's sword leaves its scabbard before the word has finished.

It is a very fine sword, narrow and bright as a ribbon of water, and he wields it as Jian has never seen anything wielded. There is no flourish. There is no waste. The blade comes out of the sheath in a single motion, and the point arrives at Jian's throat from a distance of ten paces before he has fully understood that Shen has moved.

He gets the staff up. Wood rings on steel. The blow numbs his wrists to the elbow.

The second thrust is already coming. The third. Shen advances with a steady, unhurried grace, and the blade is everywhere: at the knee, the ribs, the shoulder, flickering like a swallow. Jian gives ground. He has no choice. He backs, parries, backs. The staff rings and shudders in his hands. A cut opens along his forearm, thin and bright. A second, across the thigh.

"This," says Shen, quite softly, "is what I meant."

Jian does not answer. He is counting.

Not blows. Steps. He has backed eleven paces from the center of the Ring, and the white stone edge is behind his heels. Shen knows it. He is driving him out. A man who is forced beyond the edge, by the Rule, forfeits.

Eleven steps, Jian thinks. Twelve. Thirteen.

He feels the edge. It is a thin line of black granite set flush with the white. He puts his heel on it.

Shen smiles and lunges.

And Jian does the thing that Kuang has beaten into him for a year.

He does not parry. He does not retreat. He plants his feet in a low stance, the Iron Bone stance, hips down, knees bent, spine rooted, and takes the blow on his left shoulder instead of on the staff.

The sword goes in. It bites flesh, it grates on bone, it stops. Blood runs hot down his arm. The pain is a white wall.

But the bone does not break. It rings.

Too clean, Kuang had said. Someone has been washing you.

Shen's eyes widen. He has driven a thrust into a Foundation Early's shoulder, and it should have gone through to the lung. It has stuck. He tries to pull the blade out, and it comes slowly, grating, and in that fraction of a moment, in that tiny pause of surprise, Jian's right hand comes round with the ash staff in a flat, brutal, wholly unsophisticated sweep.

It takes Shen across the ankles.

The swordsman goes down. He hits the white stone on his back with a crack that echoes round the benches, and the sword spins out of his hand and skitters across the Ring.

For an instant nothing happens.

Then the Arbiter's staff strikes the stone.

"Position," says Shen Wuye. "The defendant holds the center."

* * *

It is not over, in the terms of the Rule.

The Trial of Position runs for a single stick of incense. The Arbiter lights it at the start, and it burns slowly in a small bronze holder at the edge of the Ring, a thin gray thread of smoke. At the end of the stick, the one who stands nearest the center is the winner. Shen is down but not yielding. He gets to his feet with a face the color of paper. He retrieves his sword, and comes on again, and Jian meets him with the staff and a shoulder that screams at every movement.

It goes on for what feels like an hour. It is perhaps a quarter of one.

Shen is better. Jian knows it, and the crowd knows it. The sword-form is clean and ruthless and endless, and every few breaths it cuts him somewhere: a ribbon at the cheek, a gash across the back of the hand. But the Leveling Brew has taken the edge off the Qi in the blade, and the blade does not bite as deep as it should. And Jian has learned something in the first moment of the fight.

He is afraid of the shoulder.

The thrust that stuck was not an accident of bone. It was the Iron Bone drill, and Shen has felt it, and some part of him cannot forget. His next strikes avoid the left side. His guard drifts. He favors the right, the legs, the head. And Jian steps, with each exchange, a half-pace toward the center, letting the blade come at the ash and the flesh he can afford to lose, and giving back the ground a hand's width at a time.

The incense burns down. The smoke curls.

"Yield," Shen says, between his teeth.

"No."

"You are bleeding."

"I have noticed."

"You cannot win by position. I have the center."

"Look down."

Shen glances. His left boot is a hand's breadth outside the painted center circle.

He looks up. He looks at the incense. The last red ember is glowing at the tip of the stick, a bright point in the gray.

"Time," says the Arbiter.

* * *

The silence that follows is the loudest thing Jian has ever heard.

He stands in the center of the Ring with his shoulder open and his sleeve black with blood, leaning on the staff like an old man, and watches the Arbiter walk across the white stone. Shen Wuye's face is unreadable. He stops in front of Jian. Then, with great deliberation, he turns to the benches and raises his staff.

"By Article seventeen, the position is held. The challenge is refused. The surety stands." He pauses. "The challenger has behaved with honor. He will be so recorded."

A roar goes up. It is not quite cheering. It is the sound of two hundred people who have just watched something that will be told for twenty years.

Jian does not hear it. He is looking at Shen Yuhang, who has not moved. The swordsman stands at the edge of the center circle with his blade hanging by his side, white to the lips. The Cloud Peak Hall's pride and heir has been beaten, in front of the Sect, by a boy with a staff. And he knows exactly how.

Their eyes meet.

There is no anger in Shen's face. That is the thing that Jian will remember. There is something colder, and cleaner, and far more dangerous: a sudden, perfect understanding.

"Position," says Shen Yuhang, very softly, so that only the two of them hear. "A procedure and a potion. Not a drop of Qi." He sheathes his sword. "I will remember that, Gate Bearer. I will remember it for a very long time."

He turns and walks out of the Ring.

* * *

Bai finds him in the Pill Hall at dusk, lying on the spare cot with his shoulder bound and a bowl of broth going cold.

"You are an idiot," says the old Elder, with deep satisfaction.

"You told me to use the edge."

"I did not tell you to bleed on it." Bai peers at the dressing, grunts, and sets down a clay jar. "You will have a scar. A good one. Your mother will cry." He sits on the stool with a sigh. "Do you know what you have done?"

"Won."

"You have made an enemy of the Cloud Peak Hall." The small eyes are grave. "Not Shen Yuhang. He is only a sword. The Hall. Two Elders on the floor, a Core Elder in seclusion, and a family that has put six men into the Sect's Core in three hundred years. They do not forget. They do not forgive. And they do not fight in rings." He pauses. "You embarrassed their heir. In public. With a trick."

"It was in the Rule."

"A thing may be in the Rule and still be a trick." Bai takes a plum from his sleeve and looks at it. "I do not say you were wrong. I say you were seen."

Jian lies still. The bound shoulder throbs in time with his pulse, and under it, the seed in his dantian turns once, as if in sympathy.

"What will they do?"

"I do not know." The old man bites. "I know that Shen Yuhang has an elder brother. Shen Yuxian. A Core disciple. He has been in seclusion for nine years, on the ridge. He is not a man who comes out for trifles." He swallows. "But I have had a message from the Treasury today, which I did not expect. Elder Zhou asks me to tell you that the Cloud Peak Hall has requested a meeting of the floor. On the matter of the Gate."

"Zhou."

"Yes. Zhou, who voted black." Bai spits a pit into his palm. "I would very much like to know what he is afraid of. I think it is the same thing you are."

Outside the window, over the roofs of the Pill Hall, the evening bell begins to toll. On the ridge, in the dusk, a single lantern flickers on at the door of a house that has stood dark for nine years.
